title: Feeling and Acting: The Neural Systems of Emotion
kicker: Threat, Aggression, Regulation, Expression, and Bodily Feedback
takeaways: Behavior, autonomic and endocrine responses, and subjective feeling can vary together or separately; one physiological measure does not identify every emotional state.
Threat responses emerge from interacting circuits.
Amygdala, hypothalamus, brainstem, and cortical pathways shape learning and select among freezing, escape, and other defensive actions.
Learning changes both responses and their context.
Extinction creates new learning, while counterconditioning adds an opposing outcome; persistence and return of defensive responses depend on the tested conditions.
Aggression and control depend on specific pathways.
Hormones, serotonin, experience, and prefrontal–subcortical circuitry influence distinct actions; no single transmitter or region explains all human violence.
Facial action, gaze, posture, voice, and context contribute to recognition; observed expression is evidence about a response rather than direct access to private feeling.
Bodily feedback and social knowledge shape experience.
Interoceptive signals contribute to processing, while beliefs and social experience alter empathy and helping; these processes require separate behavioral and neural measurements.
